rationale: Tests recall of the Nuremberg Code's authorship — a clinically significant fact that the SDL explicitly highlights, distinguishing legal from professional origins of research ethics.
Checks understanding of the Declaration of Geneva as the operative contemporary ethical pledge for Indian graduates, distinguishing it from the Hippocratic Oath which is not taken in India.

Tests identification of Beauchamp and Childress as the authors of the four-principle framework, avoiding common confusion with the Belmont Report (which articulates three principles for research, not four for clinical bioethics).
Tests understanding that the four principles are prima facie — not absolute — and can be overridden by competing principles in specific circumstances, which is the key to applying them clinically.
Tests recall of the NMC Act 2020 as the operative legislation, explicitly flagging the common error of citing the old IMC Act 1956.
Tests the distinction between provisional and permanent registration — a practically relevant fact for every graduating student.
Applies understanding of 'dichotomy' (fee-splitting) as a specifically prohibited unethical practice under the Code, using the hook scenario of the orthopaedic surgeon.
Tests whether students understand that the disciplinary process for professional misconduct goes through the Ethics and Medical Registration Board (EMRB) of the NMC, not the courts.
Tests distinction between professional secrecy (broad ethical duty) and privileged communication (specific legal protection), a distinction the SDL clinical pearl explicitly highlights.
Tests the duty to maintain professional secrecy against the competing public health duty to warn — a recurring applied scenario with an HIV-positive patient.
Tests the ethical status of therapeutic privilege — the SDL is explicit that it is a contested and disfavoured doctrine, not a recognised right.
Tests distinction between therapeutic misadventure and negligence — a key medicolegal distinction for documentation and legal liability.
Tests factual recall of when the Declaration of Geneva was most recently revised — the 2017 WMA revision is the operative version relevant to Indian graduates.
Tests understanding that the Declaration of Geneva is not legally binding but has professional and normative significance — an important nuance for applied FM.
